def percentile(sorted_vals, p):
    n = len(sorted_vals)
    if n == 0:

    frac = k - lower

That's exactly the right fix, and your id() check nailed the reason. Default argument values in Python are evaluated once, when the `def` statement runs, not each time you call the function. So that empty dictionary was built a single time at import and then stashed on the function object itself (you can even see it if you inspect `tally_votes.__defaults__`). Every call that left the second argument out got handed that same one object, and because your loop mutates it in place rather than making a copy, ana and ben stayed behind and greeted cara on the next call. This only bites with mutable defaults — a number, string, or tuple default is shared too, but since you can't modify them in place you never notice. Hence the idiom you just used: give the parameter a harmless immutable placeholder default and create the real container inside the body, so each call that needs one gets a brand-new dictionary. Worth watching for the same trap with list and set defaults, and also with class attributes, where a mutable value gets shared across all instances for the very same reason.

    data = sorted(values)
